16.40. Let ∆ be a subgroup of the automorphism group of a free pro-p group of finite
rank F such that ∆ is isomorphic (as a profinite group) to the group Zp of p-adic
integers. Is the subgroup of fixed points of ∆ in F finitely generated (as a profinite
group)?                                                                 P. A. Zalesskiı̆


16.41. Let F be a free pro-p group of finite rank n > 1. Does Aut F possess an open
subgroup of finite cohomological dimension?                           P. A. Zalesskiı̆


16.44. Is there in ZFC a countable non-discrete topological group not containing
discrete subsets with a single accumulation point? (Such a group is known to exist
under Martin’s Axiom.)                                              E. G. Zelenyuk


16.45. Let G be a permutation group on a set Ω. A sequence of points of Ω is a base
for G if its pointwise stabilizer in G is the identity; it is minimal if no point may be
removed. Let b(G) be the maximum, over all permutation representations of the finite
group G, of the maximum size of a minimal base for G. Let µ′ (G) be the maximum
size of an independent set in G, a set of elements with the property that no element
belongs to the subgroup generated by the others. Is it true that b(G) = µ′ (G)? (It is
known that b(G) ⩽ µ′ (G), and that equality holds for the symmetric groups.)
    Remark. An equivalent question is the following. Suppose that the Boolean lat-
tice B(n) of subsets of an n-element set is embeddable as a meet-semilattice of the
subgroup lattice of G, and suppose that n is maximal with this property. Is it true
that then there is such an embedding of B(n) with the property that the least element
of B(n) is a normal subgroup of G?                                          P. J. Cameron
                                    16th Issue (2006)                                      101

16.46. Among the finitely-presented groups that act arc-transitively on the (infinite)
3-valent tree with finite vertex-stabilizer are the two groups G3 = h, a, P, Q | h3 ,
a2 , P 2 , Q2 , [P, Q], [h, P ], (hQ)2 , a−1 P aQ and G4 = h, a, p, q, r | h3 , a2 , p2 ,
q 2 , r2 , [p, q], [p, r], p(qr)2 , h−1 phq, h−1 qhpq, (hr)2 , [a, p], a−1 qar , each of which
contains the modular group G1 = h, a | h3 , a2 ∼         = P SL2 (Z) as a subgroup of finite
index. The free product of G3 and G4 with subgroup G1 = ⟨h, a⟩ amalgamated
has a normal subgroup K of index 8 generated by A = h, B = aha, C = p,
D = P pP , E = QpQ, and F = P QpP Q, with dihedral complement ⟨a, P, Q⟩.
The group K has presentation A, B, C, D, E, F | A3 , B 3 , C 2 , D2 , E 2 , F 2 , (AC)3 ,
(AD)3 , (AE)3 , (AF )3 , (BC)3 , (BD)3 , (BE)3 , (BF )3 , (ABA−1 C)2 , (ABA−1 D)2 ,
(A−1 BAE)2 , (A−1 BAF )2 , (BAB −1 C)2 , (B −1 ABD)2 , (BAB −1 E)2 , (B −1 ABF )2 .
Does this group have a non-trivial finite quotient?                                 M. Conder

16.47. (P. Conrad). Is it true that every torsion-free abelian group admits an Archi-
medean lattice ordering?                              V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev

∗ 16.48. A group H is said to have generalized torsion if there exists an element h ̸= 1
such that hx1 hx2 · · · hxn = 1 for some n and some xi ∈ H. Is every group without
generalized torsion right-orderable?                V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev
  ∗ No, not every (T. W. Cai, A. Clay, Preprint, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/
2504.08084)

∗ 16.51. Do there exist groups that can be right-ordered in infinitely countably many
ways?
    There exist groups that can be fully ordered in infinitely countably many ways
(R. Buttsworth).                                   V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev
  ∗ No, there are no such groups (A. Clay, Preprint, 2009, http://arxiv.org/abs/
0909.0273; A. Navas, C. Rivas, Algebr. Geom. Topol., 9 (2009), 2079–2100, with
an appendix by A. Clay; P. A. Linnell, Bull. London Math. Soc., 43 (2011), 200–
202, based on (A. V. Zenkov, Sibirsk. Mat. Zh., 38 (1997), 90–92 (Russian), English
transl., Siberian Math. J., 38, no. 1 (1997), 76–77), where this was proved for locally
indicable groups.

16.53. Let d(G) denote the smallest cardinality of a generating set of the group G.
Suppose that G = ⟨A, B⟩, where A and B are two d-generated finite groups of coprime
orders. Is it true that d(G) ⩽ d + 1?
   See Archive 12.71 and (A. Lucchini, J. Algebra, 245 (2001), 552–561).
   Comment of 2021: the answer is yes if A and B have prime power order (E. Detomi,
A. Lucchini, J. London Math. Soc. (2), 87, no. 3 (2013), 689–706).       A. Lucchini

16.56. The spectrum ω(G) of a group G is the set of orders of elements of G. Suppose
that ω(G) = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Is G locally finite?                   V. D. Mazurov

16.60. If G is a finite group, let T (G) be the sum of the degrees of the irreducible
                                        k(G)
                                         P
complex representations of G, T (G) =        di , where G has k(G) conjugacy classes.
                                            i=1
If α ∈ Aut G, let Sα = {g ∈ G | α(g) = g −1 }. Is it true that T (G) ⩾ |Sα | for all
α ∈ Aut G?                                                            D. MacHale
 102                                   16th Issue (2006)

16.63. Is there a non-trivial finite p-group G of odd order such that |Aut G| = |G|?
   See also Archive 12.77.                                               D. MacHale

16.64. A non-abelian variety in which all finite groups are abelian is called pseudo-
abelian. A group variety is called a t-variety if for all groups in this variety the relation
of being a normal subgroup is transitive. By (O. Macedońska, A. Storozhev, Commun.
Algebra, 25, no. 5 (1997), 1589–1593) each non-abelian t-variety is pseudo-abelian, and
the pseudo-abelian varieties constructed in (A. Yu. Olshanskii, Math. USSR–Sb., 54
(1986), 57–80) are t-varieties. Is every pseudo-abelian variety a t-variety?
                                                                            O. Macedońska

16.66. For a group G, let Dn (G) denote the n-th dimension subgroup of G,
and ζn (G) the n-th term of its upper central series. For a given integer n ⩾ 1,
let f (n) = max{m | ∃ a nilpotent group G of class n with Dm (G) ̸= 1} and
g(n) = max{m | ∃ a nilpotent group G of class n such that Dn (G) ̸⊆ ζm (G)}.
    a) What is f (3)?
    b) (B. I. Plotkin). Is it true that f (n) is finite for all n?
    c) Is the growth of f (n) and g(n) polynomial, exponential, or intermediary?
    It is known that both f (n) − n and g(n) tend to infinity as n → ∞ (N. Gupta,
Yu. V. Kuz’min, J. Pure Appl. Algebra, 104 (1995), 191–197).
                                                                R. Mikhailov, I. B. S. Passi

16.68. Let W (x, y) be a non-trivial reduced group word, and G one of the groups
P SL(2, R), P SL(2, C), or SO(3, R). Are all the maps W : G × G → G surjective?
   For SL(2, R), SL(2, C), GL(2, C), and for the group S 3 of quaternions of norm 1
there exist non-surjective words; see (J. Mycielski, Amer. Math. Monthly, 84 (1977),
723–726; 85 (1978), 263–264).                                           J. Mycielski

16.69. Let W be as above.
    a) Must the range of the function Tr(W (x, y)) for x, y ∈ GL(2, R) include the
interval [−2, +∞)?
    b) For x, y being non-zero quaternions, must the range of the function Re(W (x, y))
include the interval [−5/27, 1]?
    (For some comments see ibid.)                                          J. Mycielski

16.70. Suppose that a finitely generated group G acts freely on an A-tree, where A
is an ordered abelian group. Is it true that G acts freely on a Zn -tree for some n?
    Comment of 2013: It was proved that every finitely presented group acting freely
on an A-tree acts freely on some Rn -tree for a suitable n, where R has the lexicograph-
ical order (O. Kharlampovich, A. Myasnikov, D. Serbin, Int. J. Algebra Comput., 23
(2013), 325–345).         A. G. Myasnikov, V. N. Remeslennikov, O. G. Kharlampovich

16.72. Does there exist an exponential-time algorithm for obtaining a JSJ-decompo-
sition of a finitely generated fully residually free group?
    Some algorithm was found in (O. Kharlampovich, A. Myasnikov, in: Contemp.
Math. AMS (Algorithms, Languages, Logic), 378 (2005), 87–212).
                                                 A. G. Myasnikov, O. G. Kharlampovich
                                  16th Issue (2006)                                   103

16.73. b) Let G be a group generated by a finite set S, and let l(g) denote the word
length function of g ∈ G with respect to S. The group G is said to be contracting if
there exist a faithful action of G on the set X ∗ of finite words over a finite alphabet
X and constants 0 < λ < 1 and C > 0 such that for every g ∈ G and x ∈ X there
exist h ∈ G and y ∈ X such that l(h) < λl(g) + C and g(xw) = yh(w) for all w ∈ X ∗ .
    Do there exist non-amenable contracting groups?                  V. V. Nekrashevich

16.74. b) Is it true that all groups generated by automata of polynomial growth in
the sense of S. Sidki (Geom. Dedicata, 108 (2004), 193–204) are amenable?
                                                                     V. V. Nekrashevich

16.76. We call a group G strictly real if each of its non-trivial elements is conjugate
to its inverse by some involution in G. In which groups of Lie type over a field of
characteristic 2 the maximal unipotent subgroups are strictly real?      Ya. N. Nuzhin

16.77. It is known that in every Noetherian group the nilpotent radical coincides
with the collection of all Engel elements (R. Baer, Math. Ann., 133 (1957), 256–270;
B. I. Plotkin, Izv. Vysš. Učebn. Zaved. Mat., 1958, no. 1(2), 130–135 (Russian)).
It would be nice to find a similar characterization of the solvable radical of a finite
group. More precisely, let u = u(x, y) be a sequence of words satisfying 15.75. We say
that an element g ∈ G is u-Engel if there exists n = n(g) such that un (x, g) = 1 for
every element x ∈ G. Does there exist a sequence u = u(x, y) such that the solvable
radical of a finite group coincides with the set of all u-Engel elements? B. I. Plotkin

16.78. Do there exist linear non-abelian simple groups without involutions?
                                                                               B. Poizat

16.80. Suppose that a group G is obtained from the free product of torsion-free
groups A1 , . . . , An by imposing m additional relations, where m < n. Is it true that
the free product of some n − m of the Ai embeds into G?             N. S. Romanovskiı̆

16.83. b) Let En be a free locally nilpotent n-Engel group on countably many
generators, and let π(En ) be the set of prime divisors of the orders of elements of the
periodic part of En . It is known that 2, 3, 5 ∈ π(E4 ).
   Is it true that π(En ) = π(En+1 ) for all sufficiently large n?     Yu. V. Sosnovskiı̆

16.84. Can the braid group Bn , n ⩾ 4, act faithfully on a regular rooted tree by
finite-state automorphisms? Such action is known for B3 .
    See the definitions in (R. I. Grigorchuk, V. V. Nekrashevich, V. I. Sushchanskiı̆,
Proc. Steklov Inst. Math., 2000, no. 4 (231), 128–203).           V. I. Sushchanskiı̆

16.87. Let M be a variety of groups and let Gr be a free r-generator group in M. A
subset S ⊆ Gr is called a test set if every endomorphism of Gr identical on S is an
automorphism. The minimum of the cardinalities of test sets is called the test rank
of Gr . Suppose that the test rank of Gr is r for every r ⩾ 1.
   a) Is it true that M is an abelian variety?
   b) Suppose that M is not a periodic variety. Is it true that M is the variety of all
abelian groups?                                                      E. I. Timoshenko
 104                                 16th Issue (2006)

16.88. (G. M. Bergman). The width of a group G with respect to a generating set X
means the supremum over all g ∈ G of the least length of a group word in elements
of X expressing g. A group G has finite width if the width of G with respect to every
generating set is finite. Does there exist a countably infinite group of finite width?
   All known infinite groups of finite width (infinite permutation groups, infinite-
dimensional general linear groups, and some other groups) are uncountable
(G. M. Bergman, Bull. London Math. Soc., 38 (2006), 429–440, and references
therein).                                                                    V. Tolstykh

16.89. (G. M. Bergman). Is it true that the automorphism group of an infinitely
generated free group F has finite width? The answer is affirmative if F is countably
generated.                                                               V. Tolstykh

16.90. Is it true that the automorphism group Aut F of an infinitely generated free
group F is
    a) the normal closure of a single element?
    b) the normal closure of some involution in Aut F ?
    For a free group Fn of finite rank n M. Bridson and K. Vogtmann have recently
shown that Aut Fn is the normal closure of some involution, which permutes some
basis of Fn . It is also known that the automorphism groups of infinitely generated
free nilpotent groups have such involutions.                            V. Tolstykh

16.91. Let F be an infinitely generated free group. Is there an IA-automorphism of
F whose normal closure in Aut F is the group of all IA-automorphisms of F ?
                                                                            V. Tolstykh

16.92. Let F be an infinitely generated free group. Is Aut F equal to its derived
subgroup? This is true if F is countably generated (R. Bryant, V. A. Roman’kov,
J. Algebra, 209 (1998), 713–723).                                    V. Tolstykh

16.93. Let Fn be a free group of finite rank n ⩾ 2. Is the group Inn Fn of inner
automorphisms of Fn a first-order definable subgroup of Aut Fn ? It is known that
the set of inner automorphisms induced by powers of primitive elements is definable
in Aut Fn .                                                            V. Tolstykh

16.94. If G = [G, G], then the commutator width of the group G is its width relative
to the set of commutators. Let V be an infinite-dimensional vector space over a
division ring. It is known that the commutator width of GL(V ) is finite. Is it true
that the commutator width of GL(V ) is one?                             V. Tolstykh

16.95. Conjecture: If F is a field and A is in GL(n, F ), then there is a permutation
matrix P such that AP is cyclic, that is, the minimal polynomial of AP is also its
characteristic polynomial.                                            J. G. Thompson

16.96. Let G be a locally finite n-Engel p-group where p a prime greater than n. Is
G then a Fitting group? (Examples of N. Gupta and F. Levin show that the condition
p > n is necessary in general.)                                      G. Traustason
                                  16th Issue (2006)                                  105

16.97. Let G be a torsion-free group with all subgroups subnormal of defect at
most n. Must G then be nilpotent of class at most n? (This is known to be true for
n < 5).                                                             G. Traustason

16.98. Suppose that G is a solvable finite group and A is a group of automorphisms
of G of relatively prime order. Is there a bound for the Fitting height h(G) of G in
terms of A and h(CG (A)), or even in terms of the length l(A) of the longest chain of
nested subgroups of A and h(CG (A))?
   When A is solvable, it is proved in (A. Turull, J. Algebra, 86 (1984), 555–566)
that h(G) ⩽ h(CG (A)) + 2l(A) and this bound is best possible for h(CG (A)) > 0.
For A non-solvable some results are in (H. Kurzweil, Manuscripta Math., 41 (1983),
233–305).                                                                   A. Turull

16.99. Suppose that G is a finite solvable group, A ⩽ Aut G, CG (A) = 1, the orders
of G and A are coprime, and let l(A) be the length of the longest chain of nested
subgroups of A. Is the Fitting height of G bounded above by l(A)?
    For A solvable the question coincides with 5.30. It is proved that for any finite
group A, first, there exist G with h(G) = l(A) and, second, there is a finite set
of primes π (depending on A) such that if |G| is coprime to each prime in π, then
h(G) ⩽ l(A). See (A. Turull, Math. Z., 187 (1984), 491–503).                A. Turull

16.100. Is there an (infinite) 2-generator simple group G such that Aut F2 is transitive
on the set of normal subgroups N of the free group F2 such that F2 /N ∼ = G? Cf. 6.45.
                                                                             J. Wiegold

16.102. We say that a group G is rational if any two elements x, y ∈ G satisfying
⟨x⟩ = ⟨y⟩ are conjugate. Is it true that for any d there exist only finitely many finite
rational d-generated 2-groups?                                        A. Jaikin-Zapirain

16.105. Is it true that a locally graded group which is a product of two almost
polycyclic subgroups (equivalently, of two almost soluble subgroups with the maximal
condition) is almost polycyclic?
   By (N. S. Chernikov, Ukrain. Math. J., 32 (1980) 476–479) a locally graded group
which is a product of two Chernikov subgroups (equivalently, of two almost soluble
subgroups with the minimal condition) is Chernikov.                   N. S. Chernikov

16.108. Do braid groups Bn , n > 4, have non-elementary hyperbolic factor groups?
                                                                         V. E. Shpilrain

16.110. (I. Kapovich, P. Schupp). Is there an algorithm which, when given two
elements u, v of a free group Fn , decides whether or not the cyclic length of ϕ(u)
equals the cyclic length of ϕ(v) for every automorphism ϕ of Fn ?
   Comment of 2009: The answer was shown to be positive for n = 2 in (D. Lee,
J. Group Theory, 10 (2007), 561–569).                                V. E. Shpilrain

16.111. Must an infinite simple periodic group with a dihedral Sylow 2-subgroup be
isomorphic to L2 (P ) for a locally finite field P of odd characteristic? V. P. Shunkov
 106



            Problems from the 17th Issue (2010)

length function of g ∈ G with respect to S. The group G is said to be contracting if
there exist a faithful action of G on the set X ∗ of finite words over a finite alphabet
X and constants 0 < λ < 1 and C > 0 such that for every g ∈ G and x ∈ X there
exist h ∈ G and y ∈ X such that l(h) < λl(g) + C and g(xw) = yh(w) for all w ∈ X ∗ .

16.74. b) Is it true that all groups generated by automata of polynomial growth in
the sense of S. Sidki (Geom. Dedicata, 108 (2004), 193–204) are amenable?
                                                                     V. V. Nekrashevich

to its inverse by some involution in G. In which groups of Lie type over a field of
characteristic 2 the maximal unipotent subgroups are strictly real?      Ya. N. Nuzhin

with the collection of all Engel elements (R. Baer, Math. Ann., 133 (1957), 256–270;
B. I. Plotkin, Izv. Vysš. Učebn. Zaved. Mat., 1958, no. 1(2), 130–135 (Russian)).

group. More precisely, let u = u(x, y) be a sequence of words satisfying 15.75. We say
that an element g ∈ G is u-Engel if there exists n = n(g) such that un (x, g) = 1 for
every element x ∈ G. Does there exist a sequence u = u(x, y) such that the solvable
radical of a finite group coincides with the set of all u-Engel elements? B. I. Plotkin

groups A1 , . . . , An by imposing m additional relations, where m < n. Is it true that

subset S ⊆ Gr is called a test set if every endomorphism of Gr identical on S is an

of Gr . Suppose that the test rank of Gr is r for every r ⩾ 1.

abelian groups?                                                      E. I. Timoshenko

means the supremum over all g ∈ G of the least length of a group word in elements
of X expressing g. A group G has finite width if the width of G with respect to every
generating set is finite. Does there exist a countably infinite group of finite width?
   All known infinite groups of finite width (infinite permutation groups, infinite-
dimensional general linear groups, and some other groups) are uncountable
(G. M. Bergman, Bull. London Math. Soc., 38 (2006), 429–440, and references
therein).                                                                    V. Tolstykh

generated free group F has finite width? The answer is affirmative if F is countably
generated.                                                               V. Tolstykh

nested subgroups of A and h(CG (A))?

Kim Sang-hyun and Koberda Thomas published "Non-freeness of Groups Generated by Two Parabolic Elements with Small Rational Parameters" in the Michigan Mathematical Journal (2022).

The paper's key results are: Given two parabolic elements in SL(2,ℂ) parameterized by a rational number s/r, the group they generate is shown to be non-free for all numerators s ≤ 27 (with a partial exception at s = 24). For larger numerators, density estimates are provided.

More specifically, for a rational number q = s/r in (-4, 4), considering two 2×2 matrices a = ((1, 0), (1, 1)) and b = ((1, q), (0, 1)), the group <a, b> is non-free if s ≤ 27 and s ≠ 24, and if s = 24, the same statements hold for almost all r in the sense of natural density, with density estimates provided when s > 27.

The proofs combine algebraic arguments with computer-assisted verification, contributing to the broader question of when two-generator subgroups of SL(2,ℂ) fail to be free.

## Related Research on p-groups and Automorphism Orders

If |Aut(G)| is odd, then the only primes dividing |G| are those dividing |Aut(G)|. This result is from a paper by MacHale (one of the authors you mentioned) and colleagues published in Communications in Algebra.

The question of when |Aut(G)| relates to |G| for finite p-groups has been extensively studied. ## Kourovka Notebook, issues 14–16 (file lines 3163–4883): tractable-problem triage

Read completely. Problems already marked answered (∗ with "Yes/No/…" comment) were skipped: 14.4, 14.5(b,d), 14.19, 14.20, 14.23, 14.54, 14.69(a), 14.85, 14.98, 14.102, 15.14(b), 15.19(b), 15.26, 15.40, 15.45(a), 15.53, 15.70, 15.80, 16.11, 16.48, 16.51. Everything below is still open in the 21st edition.

### Candidates, ranked by tractability score

**1. 16.60 (MacHale) — score 4.** Lines 4675–4681. T(G) = sum of irreducible character degrees; for α ∈ Aut G let S_α = {g : α(g) = g⁻¹}. Is T(G) ≥ |S_α| always? (For α = id this is the classical Frobenius–Schur bound T(G) ≥ #involutions+1; the Aut-version is open.)
Attack: GAP loop over all SmallGroups of order ≤ 511 (and selected larger orders): `AutomorphismGroup`, for each automorphism (reps up to conjugacy in Aut G suffice) count inverted elements, compare with `Sum(CharacterDegrees)`. Pure finite search; a counterexample settles it, and the search is cheap enough to cover every order ≤ 1000 except 512/768.

**2. 15.2(a)+(b) (Isaacs) — score 4.** Lines 3789–3801. x is nonvanishing if χ(x) ≠ 0 for all χ ∈ Irr(G). (a) In a solvable G, must a nonvanishing element of even order lie in F(G)? (odd order: yes, Isaacs–Navarro–Wolf.) (b) Which nonabelian simple groups have nontrivial nonvanishing elements (A7 does)?
Attack: (a) loop over solvable groups of order ≤ 2000 (skip prime-power orders, 512, 1024, 1536), `CharacterTable`, find columns with no zero, test `in FittingSubgroup`. (b) is a direct scan of every table in CTblLib (all sporadic, ATLAS Lie-type, A_n up to large n via `CharacterTable("Symmetric"/"Alternating")`): a complete answer for all groups with library tables is a well-defined special case; A_n can then be attacked with Murnaghan–Nakayama vanishing criteria.

**3. 14.44 (Kazarin–Sangroniz) — score 4.** Lines 3440–3444. G = AB with gcd(|A|,|B|) = 1: is k(G) ≤ k(A)k(B)? (Fails without coprimeness; true if A or B normal.)
Attack: for every non-prime-power order ≤ 2000 (minus 512/1024/1536), take conjugacy classes of subgroups, pick pairs with coprime orders multiplying to |G| (then G = AB automatically), compare `NrConjugacyClasses`. Add the coprime factorisations of simple groups (Arad–Fisman / Liebeck–Praeger–Saxl list: A_p = A_{p−1}·C_p, L2(q) cases, etc.) via character tables. Counterexample or exhaustive small-order verification in a day.

**4. 16.14 (Berkovich) — score 4.** Lines 4491–4492. Finite 2-group with Ω1(G) ≤ Z(G): is rank(G/G²) ≤ 2·rank Z(G)?
Attack: loop over all 2-groups of order ≤ 2^8 (56 092) and 2^9 (10.5 M, feasible on 20 cores with the cheap tests `Omega`, `Centre`, `RankPGroup(G/Frattini)`). A counterexample settles it; a "yes" at these orders is at least strong evidence and might suggest a proof.

**5. 15.74 (Pálfy) — score 4 for the first open case p = 5.** Lines 4240–4242. For each prime p find a p-group of class p whose normal-subgroup lattice does not embed in the subgroup lattice of any abelian group (done for p = 2, 3; class < p is impossible by the Lazard/Baer correspondence).
Attack: enumerate 5-groups of class 5 of order 5^6, 5^7 (SmallGroups), compute `NormalSubgroups` lattice, test the Arguesian identity (subgroup lattices of abelian groups are Arguesian; also Haiman's higher Arguesian identities). Modular-lattice pruning keeps the 6-tuple search small. One non-Arguesian example settles p = 5.

**6. 14.74 (Pyber) — score 3.** Lines 3613–3615. Is k(G) ≤ ∏ k(P_i) over Sylow subgroups of G?
Attack: same loop as item 3 (trivial for p-groups): `NrConjugacyClasses(G)` vs product over `SylowSubgroup`. Then simple/almost-simple groups from CTblLib with Sylow subgroups computed in permutation representations. Cheap; counterexample unlikely at small orders but the search is complete and fast.

**7. 15.29 (Mann) / 16.63 (MacHale) — score 3.** Lines 3927–3929 / 4684–4685. Is D8 the only nontrivial p-group with G ≅ Aut G? Is there a p-group of odd order with |Aut G| = |G|?
Attack: `AutPGrp` over all groups of order 3^7, 3^8 (1.4 M), 5^6, 5^7, 7^6, 2^8, 2^9; filter |Aut G| = |G| (equivalently |Out G| = |Z(G)|, Aut G a p-group). Note the divisibility conjecture |G| | |Aut G| fails in general (González-Sánchez–Jaikin-Zapirain), so examples may exist but probably above library range; hits would be decisive.

**8. 15.30 (Berkovich) — score 3.** Lines 3933–3934. Is every finite abelian p-group the Schur multiplier of some nonabelian p-group?
Attack: tabulate `AbelianInvariantsMultiplier` for all groups of order p^n (p = 2,3,5; n ≤ 7) to see what occurs; then build a construction from metacyclic p-groups (cyclic multiplier of prescribed order, explicit formulas) and the Künneth formula M(G×H) = M(G)×M(H)×(G^ab⊗H^ab). Likely a short constructive answer.

**9. 15.3 (Isaacs) — score 3.** Lines 3803–3810. Does a solvable group have faithful nonlinear irreducible α, β with αβ irreducible? (Nonsolvable examples: SL2(5), A_{n²}; Isaacs 2000 gives evidence for "no".)
Attack: loop over solvable SmallGroups (orders ≤ 2000 minus big 2-power orders), compute tables, test all pairs of faithful nonlinear irreducibles with α(1)β(1) dividing |G| via `ScalarProduct`. Full search in a day; a "no" proof needs theory.

**10. 15.99 (Shi) — score 3.** Lines 4404–4407. Does f(n) = k (number of groups of order n) have a solution for every k? Verified for k ≤ 1000.
Attack: extend the verified range with `NumberSmallGroups`, the Cubefree package, and closed formulas for orders p^a q, squarefree, etc.; search n with few prime factors so f(n) is small and controllable. A day gives k ≤ 10^4–10^5, not a proof.

**11. 16.26 (Vasil'ev) — score 3.** Lines 4537–4542. Is there k such that no k pairwise non-isomorphic simple groups share the same prime (Gruenberg–Kegel) graph? Conjecture k = 5 (i.e., at most 4 share).
Attack: compute GK-graphs of all simple groups up to a large order bound using Buturlakin's spectrum formulas / CTblLib tables, and search for 5 groups with a common graph (refutes the conjectured k = 5). Proving a bound needs theory.

**12. 15.83 (Merzlyakov/Sosnovskii) — score 3.** Lines 4292–4295. Is there rational α, |α| < 2, with ⟨(1 α;0 1),(1 0;α 1)⟩ free? Conjugating gives the (1,λ) normalization with λ = α²; Kim–Koberda (Michigan Math. J. 2022) proved non-freeness for λ = s/r with s ≤ 27 (s ≠ 24), i.e., α = p/q with p ≤ 5 is done; open for p ≥ 6 (α = 6/5, 7/4, 7/5, 7/6, 9/5, 11/6, …).
Attack: computer search for relations for specific new α (exact rational arithmetic word enumeration, Chorna–Geller–Shpilrain / Kim–Koberda techniques). Settles individual α; not the general question.

**13. 15.84 (Sosnovskii) — score 3.** Lines 4300–4306. Rational α, β, γ each with |·| < 3 such that (1 α;0 1), (1 0;β 1), (1−γ −γ; γ 1+γ) generate a free group of rank 3? (Three parabolics fixing ∞, 0, −1.)
Attack: computer-assisted ping-pong: search rational parameters near 3 with disjoint fundamental domains in the upper half-plane, verified by interval arithmetic. A positive answer is plausibly obtainable in a day.

**14. 15.95 (Mann–Praeger) — score 3.** Lines 4373–4377. Transitive p-group all of whose fixed-point-free elements have order p: must it have exponent p? True for p = 2, 3.
Attack: first open case p = 5: search groups of order 5^6, 5^7 with each core-free subgroup H (action on cosets), check derangements' orders vs exponent; also transitive groups of degree 25 from TransitiveGroups. A counterexample settles "no".

**15. 16.33 (Glauberman) — score 3.** Lines 4569–4580. p-group with abelian A of order p^n: does it contain abelian B of order p^n normal in ⟨B^G⟩, for p = 3 (a) and p = 2 (b); elementary abelian version for p = 3 (c)? (True for larger p; D32 kills (c) for p = 2.)
Attack: all 3-groups of order ≤ 3^8 and 2-groups ≤ 2^9: compute maximal abelian subgroup order, then test each abelian B of that order for B ⊴ `NormalClosure(G,B)`. A counterexample is possible in this range.

**16. 14.67 (Mukhamet'yanov–Fomin) — score 3.** Lines 3553–3556. a ≠ 1 with |C_G(a)| maximal among nontrivial elements; H nilpotent normalized by C_G(a): is H ≤ C_G(a)? (True if H abelian or H a p'-group for p ∈ π(Z(C_G(a))).)
Attack: loop over groups of order ≤ 1000: find such a, then for every conjugacy class of nilpotent subgroups H test whether `Normalizer(G,H)` contains a conjugate of C_G(a) and H ⊄ that conjugate. Complete finite search.

**17. 16.46 (Conder) — score 3.** Lines 4632–4643. Explicit 6-generator, 20-relator presentation K (index-8 subgroup of an amalgam of arc-transitive groups on the 3-valent tree): does K have a nontrivial finite quotient?
Attack: `LowIndexSubgroupsFpGroup` up to index 40+, `GQuotients` onto all simple groups of order ≤ 10^7, p-quotient/soluble-quotient algorithms, and quotients modulo the normal closure of subwords. Any hit answers "yes"; "no" would be a striking finitely presented group with no finite quotients and is out of reach.

**18. 16.45 (Cameron) — score 3.** Lines 4618–4630. b(G) = max minimal-base size over all permutation representations; μ′(G) = max size of an independent set. Is b(G) = μ′(G)? (b ≤ μ′ known; equality for S_n.) Equivalent: maximal Boolean lattice B(n) meet-embedded in the subgroup lattice can be chosen with normal bottom.
Attack: for small groups compute μ′(G) (independent subsets via subgroup lattice) and the lattice-embedding version; scan orders ≤ 200–300 for a counterexample.

**19. 16.95 (Thompson) — score 3.** Lines 4823–4826. Conjecture: for any A ∈ GL(n,F) there is a permutation matrix P with AP cyclic (minimal = characteristic polynomial).
Attack: exhaustive check over GL(n,q) for (n,q) ∈ {(3,2),(3,3),(4,2),(4,3),(5,2),(3,4),(3,5)} (|GL(4,3)|·24 ≈ 6·10^8 cheap tests in C). A counterexample over a small field refutes it instantly; otherwise evidence only.

**20. 15.75(b) (Plotkin) — score 3.** Lines 4245–4247. u_1 = [x,y], u_{n+1} = [[u_n,x],[u_n,y]]: is a finite group solvable iff it satisfies some identity u_n = 1? (The BGGKPP theorem uses a different sequence; this one is open.)
Attack: for minimal simple groups (L2(2^p), L2(3^p), L2(p), Sz(2^p), L3(3)) find x, y with u_n(x,y) ≠ 1 for all n — search fixed points u = [[u,x],[u,y]] ≠ 1 in L2(q) for small q with GAP, then push to all q by the BGGKPP algebraic-geometry/Lang–Weil method (Singular). Computational step is a day; the general argument a few more.

**21. 14.69(b),(c),(d) (Nuzhin) — score 3.** Lines 3564–3575. For each finite simple group, the minimal number of generating involutions that are (b) all conjugate; (c) conjugate with product 1; (d) conjugate with two commuting. (Part (a) is solved; Ward's thesis has partial results.)
Attack: for all ATLAS groups compute via class structure constants (`ClassMultiplicationCoefficient`) and Möbius-type counting whether 3 (for b), 4 (for c: three conjugate involutions with product 1 generate a dihedral group), 3 or 4 (for d) suffice; produces complete tables for sporadic groups and small Lie type. Full families need theory.

**22. 16.29 (Vdovin) — score 3.** Lines 4551–4558. Which simple groups of Lie type satisfy: for every semisimple abelian A and proper H there is x with A^x ∩ H = 1? (Exception L2(5), A = 2², H = 5:2.)
Attack: for L2(q), L3(q), U3(q), Sp4(q), G2(q) of order ≤ 10^7 enumerate abelian semisimple subgroups up to conjugacy and maximal subgroups, test by orbit computations; gives the complete list of small exceptions.

**23. 15.11 (Morigi) — score 3.** Lines 3833–3835. Is every finite abelian p-group the group of all power automorphisms Pot(G) of some group?
Attack: compute Pot(G) (automorphisms fixing every cyclic subgroup) for groups of order ≤ 500; collect which abelian p-groups occur (Pot(G×H) = Pot(G)×Pot(H) for coprime orders); then aim for a construction. Good exploratory computation, uncertain finish.

**24. 14.91 (Fernández-Alcober) — score 3.** Lines 3688–3689. Hall's formula k(P) = n(p²−1) + p^e + a(p²−1)(p−1) (|P| = p^{2n+e}) defines the abundance a. Do p-groups of every abundance a ≥ 0 exist?
Attack: compute abundance for all groups of order ≤ 3^8, 5^7, 7^7, 2^9 and look at the realized set; useful recursion: a(P×C_p) = ⌊m/2⌋ + p·a(P). Missing small values would sharpen the problem; a general family would settle it.

**25. 16.76 (Nuzhin) — score 3.** Lines 4744–4746. In which groups of Lie type in characteristic 2 is the maximal unipotent subgroup U strictly real (every nontrivial element inverted by an involution of U)?
Attack: GAP over small q and rank (`SylowSubgroup`, `IsConjugate` with involution witnesses) for A_n, B_n, D_n, G2, F4, ²B2, ²F4, ³D4; the pattern in q and type usually stabilizes quickly and can then be proved.

Lower-scored but noted (score 2): 16.3 (classes of distinct sizes ⇒ S3; only the nonsolvable case remains, theory-bound), 16.4 (Arad–Herzog; largely done by Guralnick–Malle–Tiep, remaining cases theoretical), 16.1(c) (commuting-graph isomorphism vs solvability; nauty search over orders ≤ 1000 is possible but counterexamples are unlikely small), 14.95 (class-breadth, p odd; small orders already scanned), 15.48 (SLP length < 2 log₂|G|; minimal SLP length is expensive to compute), 15.67 (three involutions, two commuting, for Sp_{2n}(Z), orthogonal groups, F4(Z); needs Nuzhin-style word searches), 16.53 (d(⟨A,B⟩) ≤ d+1; counterexamples would need large rank).

### Top 5

1. **16.60** — pure finite search over Aut G and character degrees; cheapest complete test with real chance of a counterexample.
2. **15.2(a)/(b)** — character-table scans (SmallGroups + CTblLib) give either a solvable counterexample or a full table of simple groups with nonvanishing elements.
3. **14.44** (with 14.74 as a free by-product) — exhaustive coprime-factorization search over all groups of order ≤ 2000 plus simple-group factorizations.
4. **15.74, case p = 5** — finite lattice computation (Arguesian test on normal-subgroup lattices of 5-groups of class 5) that would settle the first open prime.
5. **16.14** — a complete scan of 2-groups up to order 2^9 either produces a counterexample or strong evidence toward a proof.

Sources consulted for status checks: [Kim–Koberda, non-freeness for small rational parameters](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.06375), [Koberda research page](https://sites.google.com/view/koberdat/research), [accumulation points of non-free rationals](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.10422), [new sequences of non-free rational points](http://www.numdam.org/articles/10.5802/crmath.230/), [Non-free groups generated by two 2×2 matrices](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/canadian-journal-of-mathematics/article/nonfree-groups-generated-by-two-2-x-2-matrices/387675E89A66818D7022008D63DA21AB), [Freeness and S-arithmeticity of rational Möbius groups](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/359648210_Freeness_and_S-arithmeticity_of_rational_Mobius_groups), [order of Aut of a finite group (MacHale et al.)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00927872.2010.504679), [finite p-groups with small automorphism group](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.5772), [non-vanishing elements in finite groups](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1603.04051), [non-vanishing elements and complex …](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.11313), [criterion of unrecognizability by GK graph](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0021869321005974), [combinatorial properties of GK graphs](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.04789), [prime graph with unique nonabelian composition factor](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2109.05860).
